     8	# An inherited key is resolved from the raw pairs, as of the observation time of the row that inherits it
     9	
    10	## Context and Problem Statement
    11	
    12	Slice 1 built a bridge with one entity and no relationships. ADR 0002 asserted that one shared
    13	bridge is safe because keys inherit along many-to-one edges while measures do not, and said in as
    14	many words that the walk had zero edges and the property was asserted rather than exercised. This
    15	slice is the first with an edge: an order is placed by a customer, and the question groups the
    16	freight of an order by the *customer's* country, which exists nowhere on the order.
    17	
    18	So the generator has to get `customer_key` onto an order row. The engine offers four places to get
    19	it from, they do not agree with each other, and the names do not say which is which. A probe built
    20	a two-entity model with one relationship, changed a foreign key, and read every object the engine
    21	produced. It overturned two things ADR 0002 states as fact.
    22	
    23	**The relationship view is a *current* view, not a historical one.** ADR 0002 says reading it would
    24	lose a row whose foreign key changed. That is not what happens. The macro behind
    25	`dab.view_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` is:
    26	
    27	```sql
    28	rank() OVER (PARTITION BY <SRC>_key, type_key ORDER BY eff_tmstp DESC, ver_tmstp DESC) AS nbr
    29	... WHERE nbr = 1 AND row_st = 'Y'
    30	```
    31	
    32	Partitioned by the child, so the child never drops out — it is re-pointed. After the probe moved
    33	CH1 from P1 to P2, the pair table held both rows with `row_st = 'Y'` and the view held `CH1|P2`
    34	alone. Nothing is lost; the *old* pair is what is lost, for every row of that child, retroactively.
    35	The reason to read the raw pairs is therefore history, not disappearance, and ADR 0002 got the
    36	right answer from the wrong mechanism.
    37	
    38	**`view_<entity>_with_rel` does carry relationship keys — on the target side, and it fans out.**
    39	ADR 0002 says its column list is byte-identical to `view_<entity>`. That is true only for the
    40	relationship's *source* entity. Once an entity is a relationship *target*, its `_with_rel` view
    41	becomes a double left join through the pair macro and gains the source entity's key **and every one
    42	of its attributes**, one row per child. The probe measured the consequence:
    43	`sum(CHILD_AMOUNT)` over `view_PARENT_with_rel` returned 200.75 against a true 150.75. That is a
    44	live fan trap in a view whose name invites exactly the join that springs it.
    45	
    46	**`rank()` is not `row_number()`, so a tie returns both rows.** The probe's CH5 had two parent codes
    47	in one load, so two pair rows shared an `eff_tmstp`, and the relationship view returned CH5 twice.
    48	A child appearing twice in the bridge multiplies its measures — the precise failure the bridge
    49	exists to prevent, arriving from the engine's own view rather than from anything we wrote.
    50	
    51	**The model cannot say that an edge is many-to-one.** This is the finding that decides how the rule
    52	is enforced, and it is settled by the engine's own error rather than inferred: adding
    53	`cardinality:` to a relationship is rejected with *"Valid fields are: name, definition, description,
    54	source, target, source_entity_id, target_entity_id, type"*, and that list is the whole grammar. The
    55	one candidate, `type`, is not a cardinality slot — it accepts any string without validation
    56	(`1:N`, `MANY_TO_ONE`, `BOGUS_VALUE` all pass `check model`) and is **dropped on compile**: it does
    57	not appear in the compiled `model.json` and never reaches the engine. Nor is the engine merely
    58	silent about cardinality. It is agnostic by design: it treats a child's parents as a *set*,
    59	aggregating all target keys per `(source key, eff_tmstp)` into a fingerprint and writing a row when
    60	that set changes. Many-to-many is a supported case, not a defect.
    61	
    62	So the generator cannot learn "many-to-one" from the model, and it cannot learn it from the data,
    63	because the data is legitimately allowed to be many-to-many. Something else has to say it.
    64	
    65	## Decision Drivers
    66	
    67	* a measure summed over the bridge is additive at every grain, whatever the model's shape
    68	* a bridge row is true as of one instant, and every column on it is true as of that same instant
    69	* the generator reads objects whose behaviour has been observed, never ones whose names suggest it
    70	* a case the design cannot handle fails the build loudly rather than answering a question wrongly
    71	* the walk works for zero edges, one edge and, later, a chain — without a special case per depth
    72	
    73	## Considered Options
    74	
    75	* `dab.view_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` — the engine's ranked relationship view
    76	* `dab.v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` — the raw pairs plus a relationship name, ranked here
    77	* `dab.<SRC>_<TGT>_x` — the pair table directly, with `dab__meta` for the type key
    78	* `dab.view_<TGT>_with_rel` — the view named as though it were for this
    79	
    80	## Decision Outcome
    81	
    82	Chosen option: **`dab.v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>`, ranked in the generated SQL as of the child row's own
    83	`_observed_at`, one parent per child, with the tie refused by a data check.**
    84	
    85	`v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` is the raw pair table joined to the engine's metadata to add a `rel_name`
    86	column, with no ranking and no `row_st` filter. That is what makes it the right source: the pairs
    87	arrive unfiltered, and the as-of rule is ours and visible in the generated SQL rather than the
    88	vendor's and hidden in a macro. It also solves a naming problem the pair table has on its own — the
    89	pair table is named `<SRC>_<TGT>_x` from the *entity pair*, not from the relationship, so two
    90	relationships between the same two entities land in one table separated only by a `type_key` whose
    91	meaning lives in `dab__meta.atom_contx_desc`. Filtering on `rel_name` says what is meant; filtering
    92	on `type_key = 1` says nothing and breaks when a second edge is declared.
    93	
    94	**As of `_observed_at`, not as of now.** The stage picks a version of the child; the inherited key
    95	is the one in force when that version was observed. Today the stage always picks the child's latest
    96	version, so this coincides with the current parent and the choice looks free. It is not: it is what
    97	keeps the rule stated at the level of a bridge row rather than at the level of a table, so it
    98	survives a stage that keeps more than the latest version, which is what a snapshot event and a
    99	`_is_current = FALSE` row will both need.
   100	
   101	So the ranking partitions by the inheriting key **and its observation time**, not by the key
   102	alone. A review of this slice caught the first draft doing the latter, which collapses to one
   103	parent per key and would hand every retained version of an entity that same parent — "as of now"
   104	wearing this rule's clothes, and passing every check because today no stage keeps two versions.
   105	The distinction costs one column in a `PARTITION BY` and is the entire difference between the
   106	option chosen here and the one rejected.
   107	
   108	**Exactly one parent per child, and a tie is a build failure.** Since neither the model nor the data
   109	can state the cardinality, it is inferred from the mapping and then pinned. The inference is sound:
   110	M5 already forbids an attribute expression from containing a subquery, an aggregate or a reach into
   111	another table, so a relationship's `target_transformation_expression` reads its own row and is
   112	single-valued per staged row *by construction*. What that does not cover is one key appearing on
   113	several staged rows of a single load, which is exactly how the probe's CH5 acquired two parents at
   114	one instant. So the check is not optional decoration on top of the inference — it is the half of the
   115	argument the inference cannot make.
   116	
   117	The generated SQL uses `row_number()` over `eff_tmstp DESC, ver_tmstp DESC` and then the parent key
   118	itself, so it is deterministic and can never emit two rows for one child. `ver_tmstp` is not a
   119	formality: the engine writes a closing row that shares its predecessor's `eff_tmstp` and is
   120	separated from it only by `ver_tmstp`. Determinism alone would be a silent wrong answer, so a
   121	generated check counts children with more than one open parent at the ranking instant and fails the
   122	build when it is not zero. The two together mean the bad case is loud, and that if the check is ever
   123	ignored the damage is a mis-attributed row rather than a doubled measure. Doubling is worse: it is
   124	invisible in both of a question's acceptance queries if both are written the same way.
   125	
   126	**Only open pairs.** The read filters `row_st = 'Y'`. The engine flips a pair to `'N'` in exactly one
   127	case — the source row disappears from `das__staged`, and `FULL_LOG`'s delete branch closes it — and
   128	it keeps both rows when it does. In this architecture `das__staged` is an append-only view over
   129	parquet, so that should never fire; the filter is there because "should never fire" is not a reason
   130	to read a retracted pair if it ever does.
   131	
   132	`view_<TGT>_with_rel` is refused outright and now for a measured reason rather than an assumed one.
   133	The engine's ranked view is refused because its as-of rule is not ours to state and its `rank()`
   134	can fan out. The pair table is refused because it cannot name the relationship it is carrying.
   135	
   136	**A child with no parent keeps its row and inherits a null key.** The probe's CH6 has no pair row at
   137	all, so the join is a left join. An order the source attributes to nobody is still an order that
   138	was placed, and dropping it would change a count that ADR 0002 already published. Null is not a
   139	member: it groups as itself and the generator invents nothing for it, per conventions §1.3.
   140	
   141	### Corrections to ADR 0002
   142	
   143	ADR 0002 is not superseded — its decision stands and this record extends it. Two of its factual
   144	claims are wrong and are corrected here rather than in place, because what a record was when it was
   145	made is the thing that makes it worth keeping:
   146	
   147	1. "A changed foreign key keeps its row, which reading the relationship view would not have done."
   148	   The relationship view does keep the row. It re-points every one of that child's rows at the new
   149	   parent and erases the old pair, which is a different defect and a worse one, because it is
   150	   invisible.
   151	2. "`view_<entity>_with_rel` carries no relationship key columns at all; its column list is
   152	   byte-identical to `view_<entity>`." True on the source side only. On the target side it carries
   153	   the source entity's key and attributes, fanned out. **ADR 0004 repeats the same claim** —
   154	   "`view_<entity>_with_rel` carries no relationship keys despite its name" — and is corrected
   155	   here too, not there.
   156	
   157	A third claim, in this record's own first draft, was corrected a commit later: it was written
   158	from a partial reading of the probe that produced it. What that cost is worth naming, because it
   159	is the failure mode this whole arrangement is meant to catch — the decision it reached was the
   160	one the full report supports, so nothing downstream was wrong, and it was right by luck rather
   161	than by reading. The findings it had missed changed how the decision is *enforced*, not what it
   162	is.
   163	
   164	The check ADR 0002 installed for the second claim asserted it of *every* entity, so it fails the
   165	moment CUSTOMER becomes a relationship target. That is the check working: it was pinning observed
   166	behaviour and the behaviour was mis-observed. It is replaced by one that asserts the real rule —
   167	the source side is unchanged, the target side gains exactly the source entity's columns — which is
   168	a stronger statement than the one it replaces and would have caught this in slice 1 had it been
   169	possible to write then.
   170	
   171	## Consequences
   172	
   173	* Good, because the as-of rule is written in the generated SQL, so a reader of `dar/uss/_bridge.sql`
   174	  can see when the inherited key was true without reading a vendor macro
   175	* Good, because the fan-out the engine's own views expose cannot reach the bridge: the generator
   176	  emits `row_number()`, and the case that would have needed it fails the build first
   177	* Good, because filtering on `rel_name` keeps two edges between the same two entities in
   178	  separate pair objects. It does **not** keep them apart in the bridge, which a review of this
   179	  slice caught: a stage carries one key column per entity it inherits from, so two such edges —
   180	  or an edge from an entity to itself — would emit that column twice under one name, and DuckDB
   181	  resolves the ambiguity instead of raising. The generator refuses both shapes rather than
   182	  emitting them. Naming the column after the edge instead of the target would allow them and
   183	  would change the bridge's published contract, so it is a decision for the slice that first
   184	  needs two, not a shape to guess at now
   185	* Good, because the walk is the same shape at zero edges and one, so slice 5's two-hop chain extends
   186	  it rather than special-cases it
   187	* Bad, because the generated bridge SQL grows a ranked CTE per edge, and at three or four edges it
   188	  stops being readable in one screen. It is generated, linted and drift-checked, so this costs
   189	  legibility rather than correctness
   190	* Bad, because `v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` is an engine-internal object with no compatibility promise,
   191	  like every other object here. The pinning checks are what turn a vendor change into a failure
   192	  instead of an empty column
   193	* Bad, and not fixable here: **a foreign key set to null is never retracted.** The engine's reader
   194	  filters the pair source on the target key being non-null, so "this child now belongs to nobody" is
   195	  inexpressible — re-landing a child with a null parent writes no row, no tombstone and no `row_st`
   196	  flip, and the stale pair survives forever. The probe reproduced this. If the source ever nulls an
   197	  order's customer, DAB keeps the old customer and nothing says so. That is a property of the
   198	  engine, not of this decision; it is recorded here because this is the decision that would
   199	  otherwise be blamed for it
   200	
   201	## More Information
   202	
   203	The probe found one thing that is not used and should be, when there is a reason to. Every
   204	presentation object wraps a DuckDB table macro taking a `p_eff_tmstp` with a default, so the whole
   205	DAB layer is point-in-time queryable for nothing: `f_child_parent_x(TIMESTAMP '2026-01-15')` returned
   206	the January parent while `f_child_parent_x()` returned the current one. That is a second, shorter
   207	way to write the as-of join. It is not taken because it moves the as-of rule back inside a vendor
   208	macro, which is the thing this decision is spending SQL to avoid — but a later slice that needs
   209	as-of over several objects at once should weigh it again rather than rediscover it.
   210	
   211	`type_key` is not stable across models: it was 1 for the relationship in this probe and 17 in an
   212	earlier one, and attribute type keys differ per entity within a single model. It is never
   213	hardcoded — `rel_name` is what the generated SQL matches on, which is the whole reason
   214	`v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` is read rather than the pair table it wraps.
   215	
   216	## Confirmation
   217	
   218	`tests/test_uss.py` asserts the generated bridge left-joins the pairs rather than inner-joining
   219	them, that it ranks by `row_number` and not `rank`, that the ranking is as of the child's
   220	`_observed_at`, and that a non-owning branch still emits a typed null for a key it does not own —
   221	this last one because a union takes its column names from its first branch, so the order of the key
   222	columns is the invariant and counting them would not catch a transposition.
   223	
   224	A generated data check counts children with more than one parent at the ranking instant and must
   225	return zero. Another counts bridge rows whose inherited key resolves to no row in the target
   226	peripheral, which is the shape a mis-spelled M6 target expression takes: the engine reports nothing
   227	at deploy or at execute, and the column is simply null everywhere.
   228	
   229	The engine-behaviour checks are widened rather than removed: `_focal` and `_idfr` are still empty,
   230	`view_<E>_with_rel` is unchanged on a relationship's source side and gains exactly the source
   231	entity's columns on its target side.
   232	
   233	What this slice still does not prove is the fan-out property itself. Both entities here are at the
   234	same grain — one order has one customer — so no measure can multiply across the edge no matter how
   235	the join is written. The first measure at a finer grain arrives in slice 4, and that is where the
   236	test that a parent's measure is not multiplied by its children becomes possible. Saying so is the
   237	point: ADR 0002 asserted this property in slice 1 and it is still asserted now.

     8	# The machinery is modelled in its own typed vocabulary, and no business word appears under `src/`
     9	
    10	## Context and Problem Statement
    11	
    12	The brief asks for a domain model that does not restate `dab/model.yaml`. That constraint is
    13	easy to read as a style preference and it is not one: it decides what this repository is.
    14	
    15	There are two candidate domains here and they are genuinely different. One is the business —
    16	orders, countries, the dates on which things happened — and it already has a home, because
    17	`dab/model.yaml` is the only place the data is explained (blueprint B8). The other is the
    18	*system*: contracts, pipelines, landings, staged views, mappings, plans, stages, peripherals,
    19	bridges, questions, destinations. Nothing describes that domain yet, and it is the one the Python
    20	is actually about.
    21	
    22	The failure mode this guards against is specific. A pipeline that knows what an order is has
    23	stopped being a pipeline and become an order-loading script, and the next source needs a second
    24	one. The blog names this from the other direction: what makes a declarative platform work is that
    25	"an agent that learns the shape of one entity knows the shape of all of them"
    26	(*context-isnt-enough*). Uniformity is the property, and a special case in the machinery is what
    27	destroys it — quietly, one entity at a time.
    28	
    29	There is a real cost on the other side, and the same literature names it: over-generic models
    30	"lacking domain specificity" are one of the two named failure modes of model-driven platforms
    31	(*the-rise-of-model-driven-data-engineer*). A machinery vocabulary is a second thing to learn, and
    32	an abstraction built for slices that may never arrive is worse than the concrete code it replaced.
    33	
    34	## Decision Drivers
    35	
    36	* the machinery must work for a source and a business model it has never seen
    37	* the constraint must be checkable, not merely believed
    38	* tests must *prove* the machinery is generic rather than assert it
    39	* the model must be small enough that slice 1 does not pay for slice 6
    40	
    41	## Considered Options
    42	
    43	* A typed machinery domain model, with no business vocabulary under `src/` or in tests
    44	* Untyped dictionaries and strings throughout, with the shape documented in prose
    45	* A machinery model that names business concepts where it is convenient
    46	* A generic model built now for all six slices
    47	
    48	## Decision Outcome
    49	
    50	Chosen option: **a typed machinery domain model with no business vocabulary under `src/` or in
    51	tests**, and neutral fixture systems held as data files.
    52	
    53	The rule earns its keep by being falsifiable. "The machinery is generic" is an assertion; "no
    54	business word appears in it" is a property anyone can check by reading, and a reviewer who finds
    55	`order` in a function name has found a real defect without needing to understand the pipeline. It
    56	converts an architectural intention into something a code review can act on.
    57	
    58	Tests are where the rule does its most useful work. A test that loads a fixture called `ORDER`
    59	proves the machinery works for orders; a test that loads a neutral fixture — `PARENT`, `CHILD`,
    60	declared in a YAML file the test does not read for meaning — proves it works for *a* model. The
    61	second is the claim we actually want, and it is only available if the vocabulary stays out of the
    62	test. This is also why the question runner is parameterised over discovered question files rather
    63	than written as one test function per question: a per-question function smuggles the business
    64	vocabulary back in through its own name.
    65	
    66	Untyped dictionaries were the serious alternative, and they lose on the same ground. The types are
    67	where the machinery's own concepts are *named*, and a `dict[str, Any]` passed between six
    68	functions has no domain model at all — only a convention nobody can check. A strict type checker
    69	handles frozen dataclasses, string enums and discriminated unions with no friction, so the cost of
    70	typing is close to zero and the return is a compiler that refuses to let a `Contract` be used
    71	where a `Model` is meant.
    72	
    73	The last option — building the model for all six slices now — is rejected on the named failure
    74	mode. Slice 1 gets exactly the types slice 1 needs. No `Relationship`, no `Cardinality`, no
    75	measure kinds, no dialect abstraction beyond the single seam. Every one of those arrives in the
    76	slice that first has two of something to generalise over, which is the only point at which the
    77	generalisation can be judged.
    78	
    79	### Consequences
    80	
    81	* Good, because the claim "this works for any source and any business model" becomes a property a
    82	  reader can verify rather than a promise
    83	* Good, because the types name the machinery's own domain, which is otherwise nameless and lives
    84	  only in whoever wrote the pipeline
    85	* Good, because a neutral fixture makes a test prove genericity instead of asserting it
    86	* Bad, because there is now a second vocabulary to learn, and someone debugging a data problem has
    87	  to translate between "peripheral" and the entity they were actually looking at
    88	* Bad, because the rule has an awkward edge at the boundary: SQL generation must *emit* business
    89	  names it may not *contain*, so those names arrive as data and the code manipulating them reads
    90	  more abstractly than the thing it produces
    91	* Bad, because building only for slice 1 guarantees refactoring in slices 2 and 4, when
    92	  relationships and a second grain arrive. That is the intended trade: refactoring under a test
    93	  suite is cheaper than an abstraction chosen before the second case existed
    94	
    95	### Confirmation
    96	
    97	`tests/` contains no entity, attribute, measure, source or column name from the business, and its
    98	fixtures are neutral models held as data files. That is a hard rule in
    99	[conventions.md §5 and §6](../conventions.md) and it is checked by reading — no linter can tell a
   100	business noun from a machinery one, and a regex list of forbidden words would be a second copy of
   101	the business model living in the machinery, which is the thing this record forbids.
   102	
   103	The type gate is `ty --error all`, and `ANN` stays in the ruff selection because `ty` does not
   104	flag a fully unannotated `def`.

     8	# A business question is the unit of delivery, carried as a data file with the two queries that must agree on its answer
     9	
    10	## Context and Problem Statement
    11	
    12	At the coffee machine, "how were sales last quarter?" works, because both people share years of
    13	context. A dashboard has none of it. The gap between that question and one a data system can
    14	answer is the actual work: an answerable question names its aggregation, its measure, its
    15	dimensions and its time grain, and defines every term that two people might read differently.
    16	
    17	This system delivers in slices, and a slice is accepted on a presentation of one question's
    18	answer. So the question is not documentation *about* the work — it is the specification, the
    19	acceptance test, and the thing the page renders. That makes its format load-bearing in three
    20	directions at once, and it has to satisfy constraints that pull against each other.
    21	
    22	`dab/model.yaml` is the only place the data is explained (B8), so a question may not restate a
    23	definition — but it must carry enough that a reader can answer it without a conversation. The
    24	acceptance test compares two business queries, but no test may contain business vocabulary
    25	(conventions §6). And the check that gives the slice its confidence — computing the answer twice
    26	and requiring agreement — is only worth anything if the two computations are genuinely
    27	independent, which is a property nobody can enforce mechanically.
    28	
    29	## Decision Drivers
    30	
    31	* a question is answerable from the file alone, with no conversation
    32	* definitions are referenced, never restated, and every reference is proved to resolve
    33	* the acceptance test names nothing from the business
    34	* the two queries are independent enough that agreement means something
    35	* the question survives being reprioritised, refined or pivoted, which the methodology expects
    36	
    37	## Considered Options
    38	
    39	* A question directory holding `question.md` plus the two queries as `.sql` files
    40	* A single markdown file with the SQL in fenced blocks
    41	* Questions as test functions in `tests/`
    42	* A recorded expected result committed alongside, with no second query
    43	
    44	## Decision Outcome
    45	
    46	Chosen option: **a directory per question under `docs/questions/NN-<slug>/`, holding
    47	`question.md` and the two queries as `staged.sql` and `uss.sql`.**
    48	
    49	Separate `.sql` files rather than fenced blocks, for a reason that is not aesthetic: `.sql` files
    50	are linted by the same sqlfluff hook as every other statement in the repository, and
    51	[conventions §3](../conventions.md) already refuses to let SQL hide inside a string. A fenced
    52	block is a string. The moment the acceptance queries are exempt from the SQL rules, they become
    53	the least-reviewed SQL in a repository whose whole claim rests on them.
    54	
    55	*The file is a data file, and that is what keeps the test clean.* The runner discovers question
    56	directories, reads the front matter, runs both queries and asserts agreement — naming nothing. A
    57	per-question test *function* would smuggle the vocabulary back in through its own name, so the
    58	runner is parameterised over what it finds.
    59	
    60	*Definitions are referenced by identifier.* The front matter lists the model identifiers the
    61	question depends on, and the prose cites them by token rather than by paraphrase. A machinery test
    62	asserts every token resolves to something `dab/model.yaml` or `dab/uss.yaml` defines. When a
    63	question needs a term the model does not define, the question is **blocked** and the model change
    64	comes first — which is not an obstacle but the methodology working: a question the model cannot
    65	answer has found a gap in the model, and finding it is what asking was for.
    66	
    67	### What the two queries actually prove, and what they do not
    68	
    69	This deserves to be stated honestly, because it is easy to oversell.
    70	
    71	The control query computes the answer from `das__staged.<table>__current`, bypassing DAB and DAR
    72	entirely. The other computes it from `dar__uss`. CI asserts they agree row for row.
    73	
    74	What it catches is the failure this architecture is most exposed to and least able to see: that
    75	routing a number through integration and generation *changed it*. Dropped rows from a join, a
    76	multiplied measure, a mis-inherited key, a version collapse that kept the wrong row, an event
    77	filter that excluded more than it meant to — all of these show up as a number that no longer
    78	matches the source.
    79	
    80	What it does not catch is a wrong definition. If the model says an order is placed on its shipped
    81	date, both queries can be written to that and both will be wrong together. Nor does it catch a
    82	failure the staged layer shares — and there is one specific case worth naming: the engine's
    83	duplicate-row defect is invisible in every presentation view, so both queries would agree while
    84	the history quietly corrupted. That is why a separate data check counts the base table directly.
    85	
    86	The risk that the two are written to agree rather than to be right is real and cannot be designed
    87	away. Three things reduce it. The queries read different schemas in different vocabularies, so a
    88	transcription is visible as one. The control query is forbidden from mentioning `dab` or
    89	`dar__uss`, so it cannot consult the answer it is checking. And when they disagree,
    90	`dab/model.yaml` is the named arbiter: the query that departs from the definition is the one that
    91	changes, never both until they match. Without that last rule the cheapest repair is to make the
    92	check agree with itself, which deletes the only thing it was measuring.
    93	
    94	A recorded expected result was the alternative. It is simpler and it catches every regression
    95	exactly — but its first recording is only as right as the query that produced it, and after that
    96	it can only confirm the system still agrees with its own past. It is a regression test, not a
    97	reconciliation, and this layer needs the second.
    98	
    99	### Lifecycle
   100	
   101	`status` is one of `draft`, `red`, `green`, `superseded`. The methodology expects a question to be
   102	validated, refined or pivoted once the business sees real data, and all three are wins — so a
   103	refinement edits the question in place and a pivot supersedes it with a new one, keeping the
   104	original with its status set. What the business asked for before it saw the answer is part of the
   105	record of why the model looks the way it does.
   106	
   107	One question, one slice, one branch, one page. The page reads the question's own `uss.sql`, so the
   108	presentation and the test cannot disagree about what was asked.
   109	
   110	### Consequences
   111	
   112	* Good, because the specification, the acceptance test and the rendered page are one artefact,
   113	  which is what makes the prototype the deliverable rather than a report about it
   114	* Good, because the acceptance queries are linted like all other SQL
   115	* Good, because a question that outruns the model is blocked visibly rather than answered
   116	  approximately
   117	* Bad, because every answer is written twice, which is duplicated effort and a second thing to
   118	  maintain when a definition changes
   119	* Bad, because the control query has a shelf life. It stays writable only while a question needs
   120	  no integration; from the first question spanning two sources, writing it against the staged
   121	  layer means reimplementing DAB inside the check. Slice 6 is where that bill arrives, and this
   122	  record does not pay it
   123	* Bad, because "independent" is a property of how the queries were written and nothing enforces
   124	  it. The arbiter rule limits the damage; it does not prevent the sin
   125	
   126	### Confirmation
   127	
   128	`tests/test_questions.py` asserts every question file parses and every definition token resolves
   129	to the model. `check_question` enforces both halves of the boundary rule — the control query
   130	mentions neither `dab` nor `dar__uss` and *does* read a `__current` view, and the answer query
   131	reads `dar__uss` and reaches past it for nothing — because the page runs the answer query verbatim
   132	and a reach past DAR would render, pass, and be exactly the dependency the flow rules exist to
   133	prevent.
   134	
   135	The declared dimensions are asserted against the **answer** query only. An earlier draft of this
   136	record claimed both; that was wrong, and the check caught it on its first run. The control query
   137	says the same thing in the source's own words, and requiring the same spelling in both would force
   138	one to be written from the other — which is precisely the independence this whole arrangement is
   139	for.
   140	
   141	`adss check` runs both queries against the built warehouse and asserts row-for-row equality. Both
   142	suites name nothing from the business.

     8	# A DAS contract is documentation, schema and transformation in one artefact, and it generates a forgiving raw view plus a strict staged change log
     9	
    10	## Context and Problem Statement
    11	
    12	Somewhere around the fifteenth staging table, hand-written SQL becomes a collection of
    13	undocumented micro-decisions nobody can reason about as a whole. A `COALESCE` wrapping a
    14	`SAFE_CAST` wrapping a JSON extraction might be handling a known source quirk or working around
    15	bad data that was hot-fixed months ago, and there is no way to tell, because the knowledge left
    16	with whoever wrote it. The contract exists to put that knowledge somewhere a person can read.
    17	
    18	Two blueprint principles pull in opposite directions here and the design has to satisfy both. S3
    19	says ingestion is forgiving and unpacking is strict: committing to a schema at ingest turns every
    20	upstream change into lost data, and enforcing nothing on the way out turns every upstream change
    21	into a silent one. S1 says DAS captures and persists *only* — no interpretation. A type cast sits
    22	uncomfortably between them, and the record has to say why it is capture rather than
    23	interpretation.
    24	
    25	The append-only rule (S2) creates the question this record most has to answer. After two loads the
    26	lake holds two copies of every unchanged record. Something downstream has to decide whether that
    27	is a change log or a duplicate, and the answer determines how DAB historizes — which makes it the
    28	most consequential thing in the layer.
    29	
    30	Two observations, both made against the real tools, close off the obvious implementations. `dlt`
    31	does not stop normalising when told to limit nesting: top-level keys are still split into inferred
    32	typed columns, and inference chose `DOUBLE` for a decimal money field. And `read_parquet` over a
    33	glob **silently drops** columns that appear only in later files — no error, no warning, just
    34	missing data — which is a correctness failure that an append-only lake will produce on its own the
    35	first time a column is added.
    36	
    37	## Decision Drivers
    38	
    39	* an upstream change must never lose data, and must never pass through unnoticed
    40	* the contract is the documentation, so there is nothing to keep in step with it
    41	* the layer must say what the source said, in the source's words
    42	* per-data-point provenance: from where, and when
    43	* every future engineer's staging decision is made once, in one place
    44	
    45	## Considered Options
    46	
    47	* One YAML contract generating a raw view over the payload plus a strict staged change log, with a `__current` projection beside it
    48	* `das__staged` deduplicated to one row per key, with the change log discarded
    49	* Letting the loader infer the schema and treating its output as the staged layer
    50	* Hand-written staging SQL per source table
    51	
    52	## Decision Outcome
    53	
    54	Chosen option: **one contract per source entity set, generating `das__raw.<table>`,
    55	`das__staged.<table>` as the change log, and `das__staged.<table>__current` beside it.**
    56	
    57	*`das__raw` is forgiving.* Each source record lands whole, as one JSON value in a `payload`
    58	column, alongside provenance the pipeline adds itself. Nothing is inferred, nothing is split, and
    59	a field the contract has never heard of still lands — it is simply not yet extracted. Schema drift
    60	becomes a contract edit rather than a pipeline failure, which is the whole point of S3's first
    61	half.
    62	
    63	*`das__staged` is strict.* One `cast(payload ->> '$.<SourcePath>' AS <TYPE>) AS <target_name>` per
    64	declared column, and nothing else. A column the contract does not declare does not exist
    65	downstream. `payload` is deliberately **absent** from the staged view: if it were present, a DAB
    66	mapping could read `payload ->> '$.X'` and bypass the contract entirely, and the contract would
    67	stop being the gate.
    68	
    69	This is where the S1 tension resolves. The cast is not interpretation, it is *transcription*: the
    70	contract records what the source's own metadata says a field is, and the cast makes the warehouse
    71	agree. The evidence that this is the right side of the line is that the alternative loses
    72	information — inference made a decimal into a floating-point number, silently, and money became
    73	approximate. Declaring `DECIMAL(18, 4)` in the contract recovers exactly what the source declared.
    74	What would cross the line is a `COALESCE`, a `CASE` on values, a filter or a default, and the
    75	contract format is structurally incapable of expressing any of them: there is no key for it.
    76	
    77	*The staged view is the change log, and `__current` sits beside it.* This is the consequential
    78	half. DAS is append-only, so the change log is what the layer actually holds, and it is what DAB
    79	historizes from — with `FULL_LOG`, which is idempotent against a multi-row-per-key source. The
    80	`__current` projection exists because a question asked *of the source* needs one row per thing,

     8	# daana-cli is the DAB engine, vendored as a checksum-pinned binary and constrained by a mapping rule set this repository enforces itself
     9	
    10	## Context and Problem Statement
    11	
    12	DAB is where the three challenges are actually addressed, and Ensemble Modeling is how: a Core
    13	Business Concept holding only identity, a Description per attribute with its own history, an
    14	Association per relationship. The point of that decomposition is that change is additive — a new
    15	attribute is a new structure, never an `ALTER` to one other things depend on (blueprint B7).
    16	`daana-cli` implements exactly this shape, generating the structures and the loading code from a
    17	declared model, which is the "consistency by construction" the architecture depends on.
    18	
    19	Adopting it raises two problems that have nothing to do with modelling.
    20	
    21	The first is supply. The binary is a 174 MB git-LFS object on a private repository's branch. CI
    22	cannot reach it unauthenticated — raw, media and API all refuse — so the engine has to get into a
    23	build somehow, and the choice has consequences for anyone who ever clones this repository.
    24	
    25	The second is that the engine accepts several kinds of wrong mapping without complaint, and two of
    26	those are silent. `FULL` ingestion against a source view holding more than one row per key inserts
    27	one duplicate row per execute, forever, and **every presentation view hides it** — the current
    28	view and the history view both stayed the right size across three runs while the base table grew
    29	22 → 23 → 24 → 25. Our staged change log is multi-row-per-key by construction, so the wrong
    30	setting is the one that looks like a snapshot loader and is named after completeness. A mismatched
    31	relationship `source_table` is skipped in silence. Two `primary_keys` entries mean two alternate
    32	identifiers rather than a composite key, and that mode cannot be undone once loaded.
    33	
    34	Three further behaviours were observed on DuckDB, which the engine's own help text does not list
    35	among its supported platforms. `<entity>_focal` and `<entity>_idfr` are created but never
    36	populated. `view_<entity>_with_rel` carries no relationship keys despite its name. And if the
    37	process invoking the engine is itself holding the warehouse open, `execute` fails with
    38	`daana framework is not installed on the remote database`, which is not what went wrong.
    39	
    40	That last one was first reported to us in a broader form — that *any* other connection breaks it —
    41	and that turned out not to reproduce. DuckDB's lock is **per process**: within one process every
    42	connection shares an instance, so a second open succeeds; across processes the second is refused.
    43	The failure is therefore specific and enforceable: we must not hold the file while asking a
    44	subprocess to write to it. The narrower rule is the useful one, because it can be checked in code
    45	rather than believed.
    46	
    47	## Decision Drivers
    48	
    49	* a clone of this repository can build it, without a secret
    50	* the engine version is pinned by something that cannot be silently changed
    51	* the ways the engine accepts a wrong mapping are closed by this repository, not remembered
    52	* the DAB layer's history is what DAS observed, and is reproducible
    53	* a misleading engine error costs a reader minutes, not an afternoon
    54	
    55	## Considered Options
    56	
    57	* Vendor the binary here under git-LFS, restored in CI from a checksum-keyed cache
    58	* Fetch it in CI from the private source repository using a token secret
    59	* Two-tier CI: the gate always, the warehouse build only where the binary happens to exist
    60	* Require a local path and document it
    61	
    62	## Decision Outcome
    63	
    64	Chosen option: **vendor it here under git-LFS at `bin/linux-amd64/daana-cli`, with its `.sha256`
    65	beside it, restored in CI from an Actions cache keyed on that checksum.**
    66	
    67	The property that decides it is that the repository becomes self-contained: anyone who can clone
    68	it can build it, with no secret, no access to a second private repository, and no step that works
    69	only on the machine it was written on. For a system whose entire claim is reproducibility, an
    70	engine reachable only by the person holding a token is the wrong shape. Fetching with a secret was
    71	the serious alternative and it loses on exactly that — CI breaks for a fork, and for a future
    72	maintainer after a rotation, in a way that looks like a code failure. Two-tier CI loses harder:
    73	the check that actually proves the architecture works would be the one that does not run.
    74	
    75	The cost is real and is accepted: 174 MB of LFS storage, and a bandwidth bill on any run that
    76	misses the cache. Keying the cache on the checksum rather than on a version string means the
    77	transfer happens once per *binary*, and a changed binary invalidates the cache by construction
    78	rather than by anyone remembering to bump something.
    79	
    80	*The engine is pinned by content.* `daana-cli --version` self-reports `nightly` with a commit
    81	hash, so there is no version to depend on. `bin/linux-amd64/daana-cli.sha256` is the pin, it is
    82	verified before every invocation, and a mismatch is a hard failure rather than a warning. The
    83	self-reported string is recorded alongside it, so an upgrade is a diff that names both what
    84	changed and what it called itself.
    85	
    86	*The mapping rules are enforced here.* The seven rules in
    87	[conventions.md §1.4](../conventions.md) exist because the engine will not enforce them, and this
    88	repository checks them against `dab/mappings/*.yaml` in the machinery suite. `FULL_LOG` is the
    89	default and `FULL` requires a proof, because the failure it produces is invisible in every view a
    90	person would look at — including, and this is the part worth stating plainly, in both of a
    91	question's acceptance queries. The safety net would not have caught it.
    92	
    93	*DAR reads the `view_*` layer only.* Not `_focal`, not `_idfr`, not `_with_rel`. That is recorded
    94	here rather than in the DAR record because it is a fact about this engine on this platform, and it
    95	is where someone will look for it.
    96	
    97	*Entity ids stay `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE`.* DuckDB preserves that casing into object names, so `view_ORDER`
    98	rather than `view_order`, where PostgreSQL would fold it. The convention survives because DuckDB
    99	resolves identifiers case-insensitively — a consumer may write either — but any code that matches
   100	names out of the catalog must normalise. Keeping the model's casing loud is worth more than the
   101	convenience: the visual break from every other layer's lower case is what makes a leak from DAB
   102	into DAS or DAR obvious on sight, which is the reason §1.2 asks for it.
   103	
   104	*Detached invocation.* The CLI refuses to invoke the engine while this process holds the
   105	warehouse, and says why. Destinations open read-only, which still holds the process lock but at
   106	least keeps a reader from writing. And the misleading error is translated: when the engine says
   107	the framework is not installed, we say the file is held, because that is what happened.
   108	
   109	### Consequences
   110	
   111	* Good, because anyone who can clone this repository can build it, with no secret and no second
   112	  repository
   113	* Good, because the engine is pinned by content, so it cannot change without the diff saying so
   114	* Good, because the seven mapping rules are checked by this repository's own tests rather than
   115	  remembered, which is what the architecture asks of every other convention
   116	* Good, because the engine's most misleading error now says what actually happened
   117	* Bad, because 174 MB of LFS storage is a real cost, and a cache miss is a real transfer. The
   118	  checksum key bounds it to once per binary, but it is not free
   119	* Bad, because a vendored binary is a supply-chain artefact in the repository. The `.sha256`
   120	  proves it has not changed; it does not prove it was ever trustworthy
   121	* Bad, because the build depends on three behaviours of an engine on a platform its own
   122	  documentation does not list. Each is pinned by a check, so a vendor change fails loudly — but it
   123	  will fail, and the fallback is a platform migration rather than a patch
   124	* Bad, because vendoring `linux-amd64` alone means this repository builds on one architecture.
   125	  Adding another is adding another 174 MB
   126	
   127	### Confirmation
   128	
   129	`tests/test_platform.py` reproduces the lock failure with DuckDB alone, no engine involved: a
   130	subprocess cannot write while this process holds the file, and can the moment it lets go.
   131	The binary is verified against the committed `.sha256` on every invocation, by `Engine.verify()`
   132	in `src/adss/engine.py`, and again in CI by `sha256sum -c` before anything runs it.
   133	`tests/test_engine_pin.py` does not hash the vendored binary itself — it is a 174 MB git-LFS
   134	object a fresh checkout need not have pulled, and section 6 says this suite touches no binary —
   135	so what it asserts is that a binary which does not match its record is refused, that one which
   136	does is accepted, and that the engine's self-report is written down beside it at all, since an
   137	engine with no version has nothing else to be identified by.
   138	
   139	`tests/test_mapping_rules.py` asserts six of the seven rules against every file in
   140	`dab/mappings/` — M6 concerns relationships and lands with the first one — including that
   141	`ingestion_strategy` is `FULL_LOG` and that `entity_effective_timestamp_expression` is
   142	`extracted_at`. A data check counts `dab.<ENTITY>_desc` against its own distinct
   143	(key, attribute, version) triples, because that base table is the only place the duplication
   144	defect is visible: every presentation view hides it, and so would both of a question's acceptance
   145	queries.

    21	
    22	As the **sales director**, I want to see how many orders were placed per order month and
    23	destination country, so that I can put sales effort where demand is moving.

    37	
    38	- **Why**: demand moves between countries and between seasons, and sales effort should
    39	  follow it rather than lag it by a year.
    40	- **What**: the count of orders placed. Not their value, not their contents, not whether
    41	  they were ever delivered.

    45	  the customer is.

    47	- **What will you do with it**: move sales effort toward the countries whose monthly counts
    48	  are rising, and ask why for the ones that are falling.

    51	
    52	Both dimensions are nullable in the source metadata, and neither is null in the recording.
    53	
    54	Both queries nonetheless take the same position, for the same stated reason rather than by
    55	coincidence: an order with no date on which it was placed has no `placed` event, by
    56	construction in the generated layer, and the control query mirrors that with
    57	`WHERE o.order_date IS NOT NULL`. A null destination country would be kept as its own group
    58	by both — the generator never invents a member, and the control does not either.

    65	asks that what was delivered and when is recorded; the picture beside the question is that
    66	record, and it is why a later reader can tell whether the answer they are looking at now is
    67	the one somebody acted on.

    20	
    21	## Story
    22	
    23	As the **logistics manager**, I want to see what freight we paid per customer country and
    24	order quarter, so that I can tell where carriage is eating the margin and negotiate against
    25	a number rather than an impression.
    26	
    27	## Definitions
    28	
    29	Every term below is defined in `dab/model.yaml` or `dab/uss.yaml` and nowhere else. This
    30	question references them; it does not restate them.
    31	
    32	- {{CUSTOMER}}
    33	- {{CUSTOMER.BASED_IN_COUNTRY}}
    34	- {{ORDER.FREIGHT_CHARGE}}
    35	- {{ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER}}
    36	- {{ORDER.events.PLACED}}
    37	- {{ORDER.measures.FREIGHT_ORDERS_AMOUNT}}
    38	
    39	## The W's
    40	
    41	- **Why**: freight is a cost of fulfilment that nobody negotiates until they can see where it
    42	  concentrates. A quarterly figure per country is small enough to act on and long enough not
    43	  to be noise.
    44	- **What**: the freight charge on orders, summed. Not what anyone was billed, not a rate per
    45	  kilo, not a count of shipments.
    46	- **Who**: the customer the order was placed by — **not** whoever the goods were sent to.
    47	- **How**: one `placed` event per order carries one freight charge, attributed to the day the
    48	  business accepted the order.
    49	- **Where**: the country the *customer* is based in, reached by inheriting the customer's key
    50	  onto the order's row. This is the first question in this system whose dimension lives on a
    51	  different entity from its measure.
    52	- **When**: all history, at calendar quarter (`_calendar.quarter_label`, `YYYY-Qn`).
    53	- **What will you do with it**: take the two or three countries with the largest quarterly
    54	  freight to the carrier, and check whether the ones that are growing are growing in orders
    55	  too or only in cost.
    56	
    57	## Nulls
    58	
    59	An order with no customer would group under a null country rather than being dropped: both
    60	queries join **left**, so the total here is all the freight the business paid, and a reader
    61	can add the column up and recognise the number. No order in the recording is in that
    62	position, and no customer is missing a country, so the choice is presently invisible — it is
    63	stated because a later load could make it visible without warning, and because the generated
    64	layer already keeps such a row by construction. Nulls are not given an invented member.
    65

    67	
    68	The two queries agree, and here that proves less than it usually does.

    71	destination country — the value already sitting on the same row, one join cheaper. **In this

    73	that inherited nothing and read `DESTINATION_COUNTRY` instead would produce this same answer,

   201	_EDGE = "-- Generated from dab/model.yaml. Do not edit; regenerate with `adss dar generate`."

   204	def relationship_checks(model: Model) -> dict[str, str]:
   205	    """One check per way an edge fails without saying so. ADR 0006.
   206	
   207	    All three failures look identical in the built warehouse -- an inherited key that is null,
   208	    or wrong, on rows that look like data rather than like a defect -- and none of them is
   209	    reported by the engine at deploy, at execute, or by a question's acceptance queries.
   210	    """
   211	    generated: dict[str, str] = {}
   212	    for edge in model.relationships:
   213	        source = model.entity(edge.source_entity_id)
   214	        target = model.entity(edge.target_entity_id)
   215	        pairs = f'dab."v_{edge.id}"'
   216	        open_pairs = (
   217	            f"FROM {pairs} AS pair\nWHERE pair.rel_name = '{edge.id}'\n    AND pair.row_st = 'Y'"
   218	        )
   219	        name = edge.id.lower()
   220	
   221	        # The generator resolves a tie with row_number(), so it can never fan out -- but
   222	        # resolving a tie deterministically is still choosing arbitrarily between two answers.
   223	        generated[f"{name}__one_target"] = (
   224	            f"{_EDGE}\n"
   225	            f"SELECT count(*) AS ambiguities\n"
   226	            f"FROM (\n"
   227	            f"    SELECT\n"
   228	            f"        pair.{crossing(source.source_key)} AS source_key,\n"
   229	            f"        pair.eff_tmstp AS observed_at\n"
   230	            f"    {open_pairs}\n"
   231	            f"    GROUP BY pair.{crossing(source.source_key)}, pair.eff_tmstp\n"
   232	            f"    HAVING count(DISTINCT pair.{crossing(target.source_key)}) > 1\n"

   238	        generated[f"{name}__loaded"] = (
   239	            f"{_EDGE}\n"
   240	            f"SELECT count(*) AS unloaded\n"
   241	            f"FROM (SELECT 1 AS declared) AS edge\n"
   242	            f"WHERE NOT EXISTS (\n"
   243	            f"    SELECT 1\n"
   244	            f"    {open_pairs}\n"
   245	            f");\n"
   246	        )

   248	        # And a target expression of the wrong shape loads pairs that join to nothing.

   252	            f"FROM {BRIDGE.sql} AS b\n"
   253	            f"LEFT JOIN {Relation(Schema.DAR_USS, target.object_name).sql} AS t\n"
   254	            f"    ON b.{target.key_column} = t.{target.key_column}\n"
   255	            f"WHERE b._stage = '{source.object_name}'\n"
   256	            f"    AND b.{target.key_column} IS NOT NULL\n"
   257	            f"    AND t.{target.key_column} IS NULL;\n"
   258	        )

   230	                f"null, which reads as 'these rows have no target' rather than as a gap."
   231	            )

   240	                f"is <SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>, so {mapping.entity_id} can load {expected or 'none'}. "

   242	                f"work, and be an edge nothing explains."
   243	            )

   248	                f"mapping loads {mapping.entity_id}. An edge is declared by the entity it "
   249	                f"runs from, because that is the row the target expression reads."
   250	            )

   256	                f"skips a relationship whose source_table it cannot match, in silence, and "
   257	                f"the inherited key is then null on every row."
   258	            )

-- Generated from dab/model.yaml and dab/uss.yaml. Do not edit; regenerate.
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE dar__uss._bridge AS
WITH placed__version AS (
SELECT
    revision."ORDER_key" AS order_key,
    revision.eff_tmstp AS _observed_at,
    cast(revision."PLACED_ON" AS DATE) AS _event_date,
    cast(1 AS BIGINT) AS _measure__order__placed_orders_count,
    cast(revision."FREIGHT_CHARGE" AS DECIMAL(28, 8)) AS _measure__order__freight_orders_amount
FROM dab."view_ORDER_hist" AS revision
WHERE revision."PLACED_ON" IS NOT NULL
QUALIFY row_number() OVER (
    PARTITION BY revision."ORDER_key"
    ORDER BY revision.eff_tmstp DESC
) = 1
),

placed__order_is_placed_by_customer AS (
SELECT
    revision.order_key AS order_key,
    revision._observed_at AS _observed_at,
    pair."CUSTOMER_key" AS customer_key
FROM placed__version AS revision
LEFT JOIN dab."v_ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER" AS pair
    ON pair."ORDER_key" = revision.order_key
    AND pair.rel_name = 'ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER'
    AND pair.row_st = 'Y'
    AND pair.eff_tmstp <= revision._observed_at
QUALIFY row_number() OVER (
    PARTITION BY revision.order_key, revision._observed_at
    ORDER BY
        pair.eff_tmstp DESC,
        pair.ver_tmstp DESC,
        pair."CUSTOMER_key"
) = 1
),

placed AS (
SELECT

    ON order_is_placed_by_customer.order_key = revision.order_key

QUALIFY row_number() OVER (
    PARTITION BY revision."ORDER_key"

),

shipped__order_is_placed_by_customer AS (

QUALIFY row_number() OVER (
    PARTITION BY revision.order_key, revision._observed_at
    ORDER BY
        pair.eff_tmstp DESC,
        pair.ver_tmstp DESC,
        pair."CUSTOMER_key"
) = 1
),

shipped AS (
SELECT
    revision.order_key AS order_key,
    revision._observed_at AS _observed_at,
    revision._event_date AS _event_date,
    order_is_placed_by_customer.customer_key AS customer_key,
    revision._measure__order__shipped_orders_count AS _measure__order__shipped_orders_count,
    revision._measure__order__ship_lag_orders_days AS _measure__order__ship_lag_orders_days
FROM shipped__version AS revision

    ON order_is_placed_by_customer.order_key = revision.order_key
    AND order_is_placed_by_customer._observed_at = revision._observed_at
)

SELECT

    'placed' AS _event,
    placed._event_date AS _event_date,
    TRUE AS _is_current,
    placed._observed_at AS _observed_at,
    placed.order_key AS order_key,

     2	# uv.lock rather than by a remote tag that can move under us.
     3	default_install_hook_types: [pre-commit]
     4	fail_fast: false
     5	repos:
     6	  - repo: local
     7	    hooks:
     8	      - id: ruff-check
     9	        name: ruff check
    10	        entry: uv run --frozen ruff check --force-exclude
    11	        language: system
    12	        types_or: [python, pyi]
    13	        require_serial: true
    14	      - id: ruff-format
    15	        name: ruff format
    16	        entry: uv run --frozen ruff format --force-exclude
    17	        exclude: ^destinations/
    18	        language: system
    19	        types_or: [python, pyi]
    20	        require_serial: true
    21	      - id: ty
    22	        name: ty check
    23	        entry: uv run --frozen ty check --error all
    24	        language: system
    25	        types_or: [python, pyi]
    26	        pass_filenames: false
    27	        require_serial: true
    28	      - id: sqlfluff-lint
    29	        name: sqlfluff lint
    30	        entry: uv run --frozen sqlfluff lint
    31	        language: system
    32	        types: [sql]
    33	        require_serial: true
    34	      - id: yamllint
    35	        name: yamllint
    36	        entry: uv run --frozen yamllint -c .yamllint.yaml --strict
    37	        language: system
    38	        types: [yaml]
    39	        require_serial: true
    40	      - id: pytest
    41	        name: pytest
    42	        entry: uv run --frozen pytest
    43	        language: system
    44	        types: [python]
    45	        pass_filenames: false
    46	        require_serial: true
=====SQLFLUFF=====
     1	# The SQL style. docs/conventions.md section 3 records why each setting is what it is.
     2	# The duckdb dialect is required, not preferred: postgres cannot parse QUALIFY.
     3	[sqlfluff]
     4	dialect = duckdb
     5	templater = raw
     6	max_line_length = 120
     7	# AL09 forbids `x AS x`, which is exactly the every-column-aliased discipline that makes a
     8	# UNION branch positionally safe. RF06 fires on every mixed-case identifier crossing over from
     9	# DAB. LT05 and LT09 are line-layout opinions a generator should not have to implement.
    10	# ST06 wants simple columns before calculations. A generated view's column order mirrors
    11	# its contract's declaration order, so the two can be read side by side; reordering to
    12	# please a linter would delete that property.
    13	exclude_rules = AL09, RF06, LT05, LT09, ST06
    14	
    15	[sqlfluff:indentation]
    16	indented_joins = false
    17	indented_using_on = true
    18	
    19	[sqlfluff:rules:capitalisation.keywords]
    20	capitalisation_policy = upper
    21	
    22	[sqlfluff:rules:capitalisation.functions]
    23	extended_capitalisation_policy = lower
    24	
    25	[sqlfluff:rules:capitalisation.identifiers]
    26	extended_capitalisation_policy = consistent
    27	
    28	[sqlfluff:rules:capitalisation.types]
    29	extended_capitalisation_policy = upper
    30	
    31	[sqlfluff:rules:convention.casting_style]
    32	preferred_type_casting_style = cast
=====LINTTEST=====
     1	"""Generated SQL is held to the same standard as hand-written SQL. Conventions section 3.
     2	
     3	Substring assertions prove an emitter said what we expected. They do not prove it emitted
     4	valid, well-formed SQL -- only the real linter does that, so it runs here over everything
     5	every emitter produces, laid out the way the generator lays it out before writing.
     6	"""
     7	
     8	import functools
     9	import subprocess
    10	import sys
    11	from pathlib import Path
    12	
    13	import pytest
    14	
    15	from adss.checks import relationship_checks
    16	from adss.contract import read_contract
    17	from adss.das import clock_check_sql, current_view_sql, key_check_sql, raw_view_sql, staged_view_sql
    18	from adss.model import read_model
    19	from adss.sqlformat import formatted
    20	from adss.uss import bridge_sql, calendar_sql, peripheral_sql, read_uss
    21	
    22	FIXTURES = Path(__file__).parent / "fixtures" / "contracts"
    23	ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
    24	
    25	
    26	@functools.cache
    27	def emitters() -> dict[str, str]:
    28	    contract = read_contract(FIXTURES / "parent.yaml")
    29	    dab = Path(__file__).parent / "fixtures" / "dab"
    30	    model = read_model(dab / "model.yaml")
    31	    uss = read_uss(dab / "uss.yaml", model)
    32	    laid_out = {
    33	        "raw": raw_view_sql(contract, Path("/somewhere/lake")),
    34	        "staged": staged_view_sql(contract),
    35	        "current": current_view_sql(contract),
    36	        "clock_check": clock_check_sql(contract),
    37	        "key_check": key_check_sql(contract),
    38	        "bridge": bridge_sql(model, uss),
    39	        "peripheral": peripheral_sql(model, "PARENT"),
    40	        "calendar": calendar_sql(),
    41	        **{f"relationship_{n}": s for n, s in relationship_checks(model).items()},
    42	    }
    43	    return {name: formatted(sql, ROOT / ".sqlfluff") for name, sql in laid_out.items()}
    44	
    45	
    46	@pytest.mark.parametrize("name", sorted(emitters()))
    47	def test_emitted_sql_passes_the_repository_linter(name: str, tmp_path: Path):
    48	    written = tmp_path / f"{name}.sql"
    49	    written.write_text(emitters()[name])
    50	    result = subprocess.run(
    51	        [
    52	            sys.executable,
    53	            "-m",
    54	            "sqlfluff",
    55	            "lint",
    56	            "--config",
    57	            str(ROOT / ".sqlfluff"),
    58	            str(written),
    59	        ],
    60	        capture_output=True,
    61	        text=True,
    62	        check=False,
    63	    )
    64	    assert result.returncode == 0, result.stdout

1	---
     2	name: dar
     3	description: Work on the DAR layer — the generated Unified Star Schema, dab/uss.yaml, and the SQL under dar/uss. Use when adding an event or a measure, changing the bridge's column contract, debugging a total that is wrong or multiplied, or when generated SQL and the model have drifted.
     4	---
     5	
     6	# DAR — data according to the requirements
     7	
     8	One bridge, one peripheral per entity, one calendar. **Nothing here is hand-written**, and a
     9	wrong name is fixed in the model and regenerated. An edit to generated output is lost on the
    10	next generation, and until then the code and the model quietly disagree.
    11	
    12	## The shape
    13	
    14	```
    15	dab/uss.yaml        the declarations: events, their dates, their measures
    16	dar/uss/*.sql       generated and committed
    17	```
    18	
    19	`uv run adss dar generate` writes them; `--check` fails if the committed SQL is not what the
    20	model produces; `uv run adss dar build` runs them.
    21	
    22	## The column contract
    23	
    24	Everything downstream is written against these names and will not survive them changing. A
    25	model change **appends**; it never rearranges.
    26	
    27	| column | what it is |
    28	|---|---|
    29	| `_stage` | the entity this row is a row *of* |
    30	| `_event` | the event, lower-cased |
    31	| `_event_date` | joins `_calendar.date_key` |
    32	| `_is_current` | always true on a transaction stage |
    33	| `_observed_at` | the DAB effective timestamp, which is the DAS extraction time |
    34	| `<entity>_key` | one per entity, in model order |
    35	| `_measure__<entity>__<measure>` | one per measure; **non-null only on the owning stage** |
    36	
    37	## The one rule that matters most
    38	
    39	**Keys inherit; measures do not.** A stage carries the key of every entity it reaches along
    40	many-to-one relationships, and a measure is non-null only on the stage that owns it. Copying a
    41	parent's measure onto its children multiplies it when summed — that is the fan trap, and
    42	avoiding it is the entire reason there is a bridge rather than one wide join.
    43	
    44	Two consequences at query time, neither of which the schema can enforce:
    45	
    46	- A join on the row's own `_stage` key may be `INNER`. A join on an **inherited** key must be
    47	  `LEFT`.
    48	- A ratio is `sum(a) / sum(b)` at query time. It is never a stored measure: an average of
    49	  averages is wrong at every grain but the one it was computed at.
    50	
    51	## Adding a measure
    52	
    53	Add it to `dab/uss.yaml` under its event, with a **definition** — the glossary copies these
    54	verbatim and never composes one. Name it `<descriptor>_<entities>_<unit>`, entity plural, no
    55	scope or aggregation words: `placed_orders_count`, never `total_orders`. Then regenerate.
    56	
    57	## Things worth knowing
    58	
    59	- The generator reads `view_<entity>_hist` and keeps the latest version **in which the event's
    60	  date is set**, so an entity the event never happened to has no row for it by construction
    61	  rather than by a filter someone has to remember.
    62	- It never reads `_focal` or `_idfr` (empty on this platform) or `_with_rel` (a passthrough on
    63	  a relationship's source side, and a fanned-out join on its target side — see the dab skill).
    64	- **An inherited key comes from `v_<src>_<name>_<tgt>`, ranked here rather than by the engine**,
    65	  as of the observation time of the row that inherits it, `row_st = 'Y'` only, matched on
    66	  `rel_name`, joined LEFT, and ranked with `row_number()` and an explicit tiebreak so it cannot
    67	  fan out. Every clause of that sentence is load-bearing; ADR 0006 says which failure each one
    68	  prevents.
    69	- **It never invents a member.** A null dimension stays null. A question that wants nulls
    70	  grouped or excluded says so in its own file, because that is a property of the question.
    71	- Layout is the linter's, applied *inside* the generator. Do not hand-format emitted SQL and
    72	  do not run a formatter over `dar/uss` afterwards — either produces a diff on every
    73	  regeneration.
    74	- A zero-edge walk is a valid walk. One entity and no relationships is the normal case.

1	---
     2	name: dab
     3	description: Work on the DAB layer — dab/model.yaml, the mappings, and the modelling engine. Use when adding an entity, attribute or relationship, editing anything under dab/, running install/deploy/execute, or debugging engine errors, history that looks wrong, or rows that multiply.
     4	---
     5	
     6	# DAB — data according to the business
     7	
     8	The layer that breaks the dependency between source and consumption. It is also **the only
     9	place the data is explained**: every definition lives here and everything else references it.
    10	
    11	## The shape
    12	
    13	```
    14	dab/model.yaml           entities, attributes, relationships -- and their definitions
    15	dab/uss.yaml             what the generated layer needs: events, measures (see the dar skill)
    16	dab/mappings/*.yaml      one per entity: how it is loaded from das__staged
    17	dab/workflow.yaml        the model plus its mappings
    18	dab/connections.yaml     one profile
    19	bin/linux-amd64/daana-cli  the engine, vendored, pinned by the checksum beside it
    20	```
    21	
    22	## Adding an entity
    23	
    24	1. Add it to `dab/model.yaml` in **business language**. No source word may appear — not in an
    25	   id, a name, a definition or a description. If you are typing the source's word for
    26	   something, stop and ask what the business calls it.
    27	2. Add `dab/mappings/<entity>-mapping.yaml`, then add it to `workflow.yaml`.
    28	3. `uv run adss dab deploy && uv run adss dab execute`.
    29	
    30	Every entity, attribute and relationship needs a `definition` written for a person. A missing
    31	one is a blank row in a glossary somebody notices in a screenshot.
    32	
    33	## The seven mapping rules
    34	
    35	They are in `docs/conventions.md` §1.4 and checked by `tests/test_mapping_rules.py`, because
    36	**the engine checks none of them**. Two are not style:
    37	
    38	- **M3 — `FULL_LOG`, always.** `FULL` against a source with more than one row per key inserts
    39	  a duplicate row on every run, forever, and *every presentation view hides it*. Our staged
    40	  change log is multi-row-per-key by construction, so `FULL` is exactly the wrong default and
    41	  its failure is invisible in both of a question's acceptance queries.
    42	- **M2 — exactly one primary key.** Two entries are read as two *alternate identifiers*, not
    43	  as a composite key, and that mode cannot be undone once loaded. Compose with
    44	  `concat(cast(a AS VARCHAR), '-', cast(b AS VARCHAR))` — the separator is not cosmetic.
    45	
    46	## What the engine does and does not do
    47	
    48	The whole type vocabulary is `STRING`, `NUMBER`, `UNIT`, `START_TIMESTAMP`, `END_TIMESTAMP`.
    49	There is no plain date type; a business date is `START_TIMESTAMP`.
    50	
    51	A version is dated by `entity_effective_timestamp_expression`, which is always `extracted_at`
    52	here — so DAB's history is what the system observed and when. That wins even when the entity
    53	has a `START_TIMESTAMP` attribute; confirmed, not assumed.
    54	
    55	## Things that cost a day if you do not know them
    56	
    57	- **`daana framework is not installed on the remote database` means the file is busy.** The
    58	  lock is per process: the engine is a subprocess, and it cannot take the lock while we hold
    59	  it. `require_detached` refuses before that happens; if you see the message anyway, close
    60	  whatever has the warehouse open.
    61	- **`<entity>_focal` and `<entity>_idfr` are created and never populated** on this platform.
    62	  Anything joining to them returns nothing, with no error. DAR reads the `view_*` layer only.
    63	- **`view_<entity>_with_rel` is two different things and its name says neither.** On a
    64	  relationship's **source** side it is a passthrough: its columns are identical to
    65	  `view_<entity>`, and it carries no relationship key at all. On a relationship's **target**
    66	  side it becomes a join back to the source entity and gains that entity's key *and every one
    67	  of its attributes*, one row per source row — so it **fans out**, and summing the target's own
    68	  measure over it multiplies. Measured on a probe: 200.75 against a true 150.75. Never read it.
    69	- **Relationship keys come from `v_<src>_<name>_<tgt>`**, which is the raw pair table plus a
    70	  `rel_name` column. Not `view_<src>_<name>_<tgt>`: that one is a *current* view, ranked with
    71	  `rank()` — so it re-points a child's whole history at whichever target it points at now, and
    72	  returns two rows for a child that named two targets at one instant. ADR 0006.
    73	- **A null foreign key is never retracted.** The engine's reader drops null targets, so
    74	  "belongs to nobody" cannot be expressed: re-landing a row with a null key writes nothing at
    75	  all — no row, no tombstone, no `row_st` flip — and the stale pair survives forever.
    76	- **`type_key` is not stable** across models or even across entities within one. Resolve a
    77	  relationship by name, never by number.
    78	- **Object names keep the model's casing**: `view_ORDER`, not `view_order`. Identifiers
    79	  resolve case-insensitively, so a consumer may write either — but code matching names out of
    80	  the catalog must normalise.
    81	- Numeric attributes are widened to `DECIMAL(28, 8)` whatever the source declared.
    82	- DuckDB is not in the engine's own list of supported platforms. It works; do not expect the
    83	  vendor to keep it working.
